newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Uncertainty prevails in Israel markets, shekel up.
newsitem.headline: Uncertainty prevails in Israel markets, shekel up.

text.p: Failure to resolve the issue of the shekel's trading bands has generated a great deal of uncertainty in Israel's foreign currency and stock markets, traders said on Tuesday.
The shekel strengthened in early trading and the Bank of Israel intervened on a small scale by buying dollars, a dealer at Bank Hapoalim said.
"Turnover is low and the spreads are very wide," he said.
The dollar was trading at 3.3850/3.4000 shekels against Monday's representative rate of 3.4160.
"The market doesn't know what will happen," the dealer said.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced after an all-night meeting with Finance Minister Dan Meridor and Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel that a foreign currency reform and budget cut had been agreed.
But talks were to continue on Tuesday afternoon on the main issue outstanding -- the shekel's trading bands.
The stock market posted early morning supply of 80 million shekels against only seven million in demand.
Traders said the weakness was due in part to a closing of positions by options players on Monday afteroon.
But the market, which is heavily export-oriented, was also strongly influenced by the currency market.
"The decision on the bands will be a major decision," Danniella Finn of Batucha Securities said.
Frenkel has pushed for a widening of the bands, which would give the central bank some relief from the need to constantly intervene in the currency market.
High interest rates have buoyed the shekel, forcing the central bank to buy huge amounts of dollars to prevent the shekel from strengthening beyond its band.
Meridor strongly opposes a widening of the band, fearing it will lead to a further appreciation of the shekel, causing the economy to slow.
Traders said the issue has now turned into a political battle that may require a resolution by the entire cabinet.
Netanyahu has dismissed media speculation that Meridor could resign if the prime minister decided to widen the bands.

"It shouldn't be a political issue, it should be an economic one. What does the justice minister or the labour minister have to do with it. They are making a political decision on a purely economic issue," Finn said.
The shekel, pegged to a basket of foreign currencies, is allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal slope designed to devalue the Israeli currency by six percent a year.
Finn said she believed that if the bands were widened the shekel would strengthen in the short term but then weaken, especially if Frenkel agreed to cut interest rates.
The central bank is due to announce next week the interest rate level for July.
Netanyahu did not provide details on the budget cut or currency market reform but Israel Radio said the cut would be 600 million shekels.
On Monday night Netanyahu said he would set a timetable for making the shekel fully convertible and for lifting most foreign currency restrictions.
